title: Sugar
subtitle: 300 BC–600 AD · Reed Honey, the Boiling Ladder and the First Roads from India to Rome, Persia and China

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Shapur I and Khusrau I — the Sasanian builders of the Khuzestan that became Persia’s cane country

entries.label: Shapur I — builder of Khuzestan
entries.hint: Reign of the second Sasanian king, who resettled captives from his campaigns at Susa and Tustar (Shushtar), founded the city of Gundeshapur and, according to Arabic tradition, brought an Indian physician there to teach medicine; a great weir at Shushtar is attributed to Roman prisoners taken after 260. The province these works built up later became Persia’s cane country, but no source attests sugar in Shapur’s own day.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Arabic traditions via Ouerfelli): al-Tabari, Ta’rikh II p.845 and al-Tha’alibi, Ghurar pp.527–531 (Indian physician; deportations; Valerian’s prisoners); Ibn Hawqal and al-Idrisi (the weir of 262); al-Mas’udi, Muruj I p.299 — all as cited in Ouerfelli, Le Sucre (2008) pp.19–20 nn.24–27. Ouerfelli asks whether these works relate to the introduction of cane (a ‘rapprochement peut-être possible’) but no text links them. For the reign itself see sassanid-224-484::k2 and the Res Gestae Divi Saporis.

entries.label: Khusrau I Anushirvan
entries.loc: Ctesiphon; Gundeshapur and the Khuzestan gardens
entries.hint: Reign of the king under whom Persian cane-growing is said to have passed from garden plots to the best lands of Khuzestan. A tradition has him learning how cane juice is pressed when, passing a garden, he was served two cups of cane juice cooled with snow — a story told as legend. His reign also saw Burzoy’s mission to India for the Panchatantra, and the Chinese Sui shu, describing Sasanian Persia, lists ‘stone honey’ among its products.
entries.note: SECONDARY + LEGEND: Ouerfelli (2008) p.20 nn.28–29 (a text of Khusrau I’s reign; cane development ‘probably from that date’); Buttery, A Dark History of Sugar (2022) p.8, citing Deerr (1949) pp.68–69 (Deerr not available to check; Buttery calls it a legend); Laufer, Sino-Iranica (1919) pp.376–377; Sato (2015) pp.18–19 (‘little is known about sugarcane cultivation during the Sasanid period’). Burzoy and the Panchatantra: Wikipedia ‘Borzuya’, context only — no sugar link. The cane-juice anecdote is not evidence of a sugar industry. See also sassanid-224-484 and roman-sasanian-world-224-632.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The siege of Pengcheng and a northern emperor’s request for sugarcane

entries.label: Taiwu asks for sugarcane at Pengcheng
entries.hint: In the winter campaign of 450 Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei advanced on Pengcheng and, according to Chinese histories, asked the southern side for sugarcane — a request that shows a plant grown only in the far south as a luxury the northern court wanted even during a siege.
entries.note: SECONDARY (primary not read): Needham, Science and Civilisation in China 6.3 (Daniels & Menzies 1996) p.63, citing Nan shi ch.32 p.829; Needham names the Song recipient ‘Sung Hsiao-Wu’ (the later Emperor Xiaowu, Liu Jun). The passage has not been checked in the Song shu, Wei shu or Nan shi.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Rome’s tariff and price lists, which name the oriental spices but not sugar

entries.label: Alexandria’s tariff lists Indian aromatics but not sugar
entries.hint: The customs tariff of Alexandria, quoted by the jurist Marcian in Justinian’s Digest, lists oriental goods subject to duty — among them cassia, ginger, myrrh and pepper — but no sugar. With the silence of Diocletian’s price edict it suggests that sugar was too rare to appear in the tariffs of Roman Egypt.
entries.note: ANCHOR (edition cited): Digest 39.4.16.7, ed. Krueger & Mommsen, Corpus Iuris Civilis I (1872) p.606, as cited by Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.26. The date is approximate: the Digest was compiled in 533, the tariff it quotes is earlier (Marcian wrote in the Severan period) and its own dating should be checked. An absence is the evidence here.

entries.label: Diocletian’s price edict names oriental spices but not sugar
entries.loc: Aezani, Aizanoi copy; posted across the empire
entries.hint: Diocletian’s Edict on Maximum Prices, set up in cities across the empire, fixes prices for foods and imported goods and includes oriental spices such as cassia, ginger, myrrh and pepper, but sugar does not appear — consistent with its being a rare medicine and not a market good.
entries.note: ANCHOR (edition cited): Crawford & Reynolds, ‘The Aezani Copy of the Prices Edict’, ZPE 34 (1979) pp.163–210, at 181–184, as cited by Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.25. The absence of sugar is reported there; the edict’s own entries for honey were not checked here.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Buddhist rules for molasses, syrup and cane juice; cane as symbol; cane in Han and Jin burials

entries.label: The Pali Vinaya’s five tonics: molasses as monks’ medicine
entries.hint: In the Vinaya’s chapter on medicine the Buddha allows sick monks five ‘tonics’ — ghee, butter, oil, honey and syrup or molasses (phāṇita) — even after midday, while Pācittiya 39 lists molasses among the rich foods a healthy monk may not ask for. The first religious status of cane products is as medicine, the same status the Greek and Roman texts give sakchar.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Pali text not read here): Vinaya, Mahāvagga VI (Bhesajjakkhandhaka) and Pācittiya 39, as summarised on SuttaCentral-derived pages; English renders phāṇita as ‘syrup’ or ‘molasses’ and the Pali wording was not checked. Needham SCC 6.3 p.68 counts sugar among Buddhism’s ‘five medicines’. The Pali Vinaya’s redaction is placed c.4th–1st century BC, so the date is a span.

entries.label: Cane on the Mawangdui inventory slips
entries.hint: The bamboo-slip food inventories from the tombs of the Marquis of Dai’s family, buried between 186 and 168 BC, are reported to carry the character for sugarcane on two slips (nos. 115 and 121), which would place cane among the foods offered to the dead in the central Yangzi valley in the 2nd century BC.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (thin): Mazumdar, Sugar and Society in China (1998) p.17, giving the slip numbers and reading; not checked against the excavation report Changsha Mawangdui Han mu (1973; 2004 ed.) or the Hunan Museum publications on the Tomb 1 qiance. Treat as a lead until checked.

entries.label: Cane as symbol, ‘nectar of the gods’ and wedding sugar
entries.hint: In Mahāyāna scripture sugarcane is the stock image of abundance — buddhas and arhats ‘as numerous as stalks of sugarcane in a field’; one monastic code calls cane juice the nectar of the gods, Mūlasarvāstivāda texts mention sugar in the marriage ceremony, and the Buddha, through the Ikṣvāku (‘cane’) line of his ancestors, is called ‘King of Sugarcane’. Such images presuppose a plant familiar to every audience.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Chinese translations via Kieschnick): Kieschnick, The Impact of Buddhism on Chinese Material Culture (2003) pp.249–253 nn.101–107, 120 (Weimojie jing, T 474 p.535b; Fo benxing ji jing, T 190 p.912a; Sifen lü 42 p.873c; Genben shuo yiqieyou bu pinaiye 25, T 1442 p.764a); Needham SCC 6.3 p.61; Mazumdar (1998) pp.21–22. Dates are those of the Chinese translations (3rd–5th centuries); the Indian originals are earlier and uncertain.

entries.label: Xie Huilian’s requiem: cane segments in the coffin water
entries.hint: The poet Xie Huilian’s requiem for two unknown dead, whose graves had fallen into disrepair, describes sugarcane segments still joined in the water at the bottom of the damaged coffins among scattered melon seeds — evidence that cane was a burial offering in the lower Yangzi in the early fifth century.
entries.note: SECONDARY (original not read): Mazumdar (1998) pp.17–18, quoting the requiem (ji wen) and its preface. Xie Huilian lived 394–430.

entries.label: Monastic rules for cane juice, syrup and crystals
entries.loc: Indian monasteries; translated at Chang’an and Jiankang
entries.hint: Buddhist monastic codes as translated into Chinese regulate cane in detail: the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya (405) allows cane juice, black syrup and soft black sugar; a Mahāsāṃghika rule says surplus cane is pressed and drunk in the evening, boiled into a syrup that keeps seven days, then heated until crystals form, which keep indefinitely; a Mūlasarvāstivāda text mentions a ‘room for boiling sugar’; other codes forbid fermented cane liquor.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Chinese translations via Kieschnick and Daniels): Kieschnick (2003) pp.253–254 nn.123–127 (Sifen lü 43 p.875a; Mohe sengqi lü 11 p.317c; Genben shuoyiqieyoubu pinaiye yaoshi 17, T 1448 p.87a; Shisong lü 53; Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra 13); Needham SCC 6.3 p.62 (the Dharmagupta Vinaya of +405). The dates are those of the Chinese translations; the Indian originals are earlier. Shimi and hui are the translators’ choices.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Chu and Han verse on cane syrup, a Latin poet’s Indian reed, and the Roman kitchen without sugar

entries.label: “Zhao hun” offers a cane syrup — or a yam sauce
entries.hint: The Chu ci poem “Zhao hun” (Summons of the Soul), attributed to Song Yu, lists the dishes meant to lure a soul home, among them stewed turtle and roast lamb served with zhe jiang. Daniels and most scholars read this as sugarcane syrup, the earliest cane in Chinese literature; David Hawkes translates it as yam sauce.
entries.note: CONTESTED (primary not read): Needham SCC 6.3 (Daniels) pp.141–142, with Liu Wu-chi’s rendering ‘syrups from sugarcane’ and Hawkes (1985) pp.106–107 for ‘yam sauce’; Wang Yi’s 2nd-century commentary is the basis of the cane reading, which most scholars accept; Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.134; Mazumdar (1998) p.17 (‘third century B.C.’). The date c.241 BC follows Daniels.

entries.label: Sima Xiangru names cane among the plants of Yunmeng
entries.hint: In his Zixu fu the court poet Sima Xiangru lists zhuzhe, sugarcane, among the plants east of the Yunmeng marshes, and a second poem has a court official using cane syrup to ease the effects of wine. Cane has reached the Han capital’s vocabulary after the conquest of the south.
entries.note: SECONDARY (poems not read): Needham SCC 6.3 pp.142–143 (Wen xuan ch.7 p.26a; the commentator Zhang Yi equating zhuzhe with ganzhe; Xu Shen, Shuowen jiezi p.18); Mazumdar (1998) p.19 and Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.134 on the hangover references (Han shu 22 p.1063). The title of the second poem differs between the sources. Sima Xiangru lived c.179–117 BC.

entries.label: Varro Atacinus on the Indian reed
entries.hint: The Latin poet Varro of Atax is credited by modern scholars with the earliest Roman line on cane: an Indian reed that grows tall as a tree, from whose viscous roots a sap is drawn that beats sweet honey. The report is garbled (the juice is in the stalk, not the root) and may even describe bamboo, but it shows Latin readers hearing of ‘honey from reeds’ a century before Dioscorides.
entries.note: SECONDARY + CONTESTED ATTRIBUTION: preserved in Isidore, Etymologies 17.7.58 (Isidore says ‘Varro’); identified as Varro Atacinus (82–36 BC) by André & Filliozat, L’Inde vue de Rome (1986) pp.8, 22, 339 n.3, as cited in Ouerfelli (2008) p.18; Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.22 gives Varro (116–27 BC) — attribution unresolved. André & Filliozat (339 n.3, 360–361 n.160) read early Greek and Latin saccharon as tabasheer; Ouerfelli (p.17) traces that debate to Saumaise, De saccharo. Strabo’s report of Nearchus (325 BC) belongs to the Ancient sugar folio.

entries.label: Lucan’s reed-drinkers in Pompey’s army
entries.hint: In the catalogue of Pompey’s eastern allies in the Pharsalia, Lucan has a people who drink sweet juice from tender reeds — an eastern custom reported with wonder, with no hint of a trade good.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Latin not read): Lucan, Pharsalia 3.237, cited by Dalby, Food in the Ancient World from A to Z (2003) pp.314–315 and in older encyclopaedia summaries; the paraphrase follows those. The Pharsalia was written c.61–65, Lucan dying in 65.

entries.label: No attested cooking with sugar in the Roman world
entries.hint: Roman recipe literature, the cookbook attributed to Apicius above all, sweetens with honey and with must boiled down to syrup (sapa, defrutum); there is no attested use of sugar in cooking in the ancient and early medieval Mediterranean, which implies that saccharon circulated in very small quantities.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021), section 1.1 (‘There is no attested use of sugar in cooking’); Dalby (2003) pp.314–315. Apicius is a 4th–5th-century compilation. This is an argument from absence and rests on which texts survive.

entries.label: Liu Yiqing on Funan cane
entries.hint: The Talk of the Times writer Liu Yiqing is quoted describing Funan sugarcane as having three internodes to the zhang, wilting in the sun and snapping in the wind — an exotic southern plant by now a literary curiosity at the courts of the south.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 pp.63, 143 n.d, quoting the passage from the Yuan jian lei han ch.404 p.5a; Needham notes it is not in the extant Shishuo xinyu, so the attribution rests on the later encyclopaedia. Needham calls the length ‘a gross exaggeration or a mistake’.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: From Theophrastus’s reed honey to Galen’s sakchar, the Indian medical texts, the Chinese botanies and the Persian notices

entries.label: Theophrastus’s three origins of honey
entries.hint: Theophrastus (c.372–287 BC) says honey has three origins: flowers, the air (moisture cooked by the sun) and reeds. Whether the reed honey means Indian cane or bamboo manna is unclear; it would be the earliest Greek hint of the substance after Alexander’s army reached India.
entries.note: SECONDARY + CONTESTED: Ouerfelli (2008) pp.17–18 (‘le texte n’est pas clair’), citing Deerr (1949) I p.63 and Desanges (2000) pp.45–46; the passage itself was not located. Ibn al-Baytar, Traité des simples (trans. Leclerc 1883) II art.1447 on bamboo manna (tabasheer). At the very start of the folio’s window.

entries.label: Eratosthenes on India’s sweet reed roots
entries.hint: In Strabo’s account of India, Eratosthenes (c.276–194 BC) says that the country’s plants have roots — ‘in particular those of large reeds’ — that are sweet both by nature and by heating, since the rain and river water are warmed by the sun; Strabo glosses this as the Indian ‘heating’ doing the work that ‘ripening’ does elsewhere. Nearchus’s ‘honey from reeds without bees’ follows in the next lines. It is a Hellenistic geographer’s account of sweet reeds, not of sugar-making.
entries.note: ANCHOR (as read): Strabo, Geography 15.1.20 (Jones’s Loeb translation on the Thayer / LacusCurtius site; the Greek was not consulted). The words ‘roots of plants, in particular those of large reeds, which are sweet both by nature and by heating’ are attributed to Eratosthenes, who is cited alongside Megasthenes on the fertility of India. Strabo does not say what the reed was; whether it was sugarcane, bamboo or common reed is open. Same chapter as sugar-1200bc-300bc::th3 (Nearchus).

entries.label: Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya mentions sugar in food mixtures
entries.hint: Mintz reports that the Mahābhāṣya, Patañjali’s commentary on Pāṇini’s grammar, mentions sugar repeatedly in food combinations — rice pudding with milk and sugar, barley meal and sugar, fermented drinks flavoured with ginger and sugar. Whether the word means a crystalline product or only cane syrup is unclear.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (thin; secondary report only): Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985) pp.19–20, who dates the text ‘c.400–350 BC’ — that is Pāṇini’s date; Patañjali is generally placed in the 2nd century BC. The Sanskrit passage and the exact word were not located.

entries.label: Dioscorides’ sakcharon: solidified honey on reeds
entries.hint: Dioscorides describes ‘a kind of solidified honey’ called sakcharon, found on reeds in India and Arabia Felix, like salt in consistency and brittle between the teeth; dissolved in water and drunk, it is said to help the stomach, bladder and kidneys. This is the best-known ancient description of the substance.
entries.note: ANCHOR (edition cited): De materia medica 2.82, ed. Wellmann 1:167.4–9, quoted in Greek by Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.22; also Eupor. 2.112 (Dalby 2003 pp.314–315). IDENTITY CONTESTED: Saumaise (17th c.), André & Filliozat (1986) read saccharon as tabasheer, a silica concretion of bamboo joints; R. J. Forbes accepted cane sugar (as reported by Mintz 1985 p.20); Ouerfelli (2008) pp.17–18.

entries.label: Seneca on honey found on Indian reeds
entries.hint: In Letter 84 Seneca says honey is reported to be found on the leaves of Indian reeds, whether as dew from the sky or the plant’s own sweet juice, in the middle of an image about how the mind digests what it reads. A philosopher’s aside shows the report circulating among educated Romans as hearsay.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Latin not read): Seneca, Epistulae morales 84.4, cited by Dalby (2003) pp.314–315; the ‘dew or juice’ gloss follows encyclopaedia summaries of the letter. Letters 84 dates to c.64.

entries.label: Pliny on saccharon from Arabia and India
entries.hint: Pliny the Elder reports saccharon from Arabia and from India, the Indian the better: a honey gathered in reeds, white like gum, brittle to the teeth, in lumps up to the size of a hazelnut and used only in medicine.
entries.note: ANCHOR (edition cited): Natural History 12.32 (12.17 in the older numbering), ed. Ernout (1949) p.29 lines 16–20, as cited by Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.22; Faas & Whiteside, Around the Roman Table (2005) p.149 via Wikipedia ‘History of sugar’ for the hazelnut detail. IDENTITY CONTESTED (tabasheer; see the Dioscorides entry). ‘Arabia also produces’ may reflect transshipment from India.

entries.label: Yang Fu’s Yiwu zhi: Jiaozhi cane and shi mi
entries.hint: Yang Fu’s Record of Strange Things says sugarcane is found everywhere in the south and that the best comes from Jiaozhi: stalks several cun round and over a zhang high, sweet when cut. Pressed, boiled and dried in the sun, the juice becomes a malt-like sugar called shi mi, ‘stone honey’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (fragmentary text, via later quotation): Needham SCC 6.3 p.143 n.d (dating it +90; quoted in the Qimin yaoshu 92/25/3); Mazumdar (1998) p.18 (translating Yang Fu, ‘first century’; she renders shi mi as ‘both solid and crystalline’ while Needham calls it amorphous); Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.135.
keywords: Yang Fu Record of Strange Things

entries.label: Ps.-Alexander of Aphrodisias lists the reed honey
entries.hint: A brief mention of sugar appears in the medical Problems attributed to Alexander of Aphrodisias, listed by Dalby among the Greek and Latin sources for sakchar. The passage itself was not read for this folio, so the entry records only that the source exists.
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (thin; content not read): Ps.-Alexander of Aphrodisias, Problemata 3.2, listed in Dalby (2003) pp.314–315; Bouras-Vallianatos (2021) n.22 cites the edition of Kapetanaki & Sharples (Peripatoi 20, 2006) p.92 lines 6–7, and dates the work first/second century AD.

entries.label: The Hou Hanshu counts stone honey among India’s products
entries.hint: The treatise on India in the Hou Hanshu mentions shi mi, ‘stone honey’, among its products — one of the earliest signs that Chinese compilers associated the substance with India, though it is Fan Ye in the 5th century who writes it down.
entries.note: SECONDARY (primary not read): Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.139, citing Hou Hanshu 88 p.2921. The treatise describes the Later Han view of India; Fan Ye compiled the history c.430, so the dating by what it describes is approximate. Kieschnick cites it for the view that at least some techniques for making amorphous sugar came from India, against Daniels’s southern-peoples argument.

entries.label: Caraka and Suśruta: cane clones, cane wine and graded sugars
entries.hint: The Caraka Saṃhitā (1st–2nd century) distinguishes a white cane and a purple-dark cane and describes cane wine; the Suśruta Saṃhitā (c.4th century) lists twelve clones, some of the Indian S. barberi group; the Bower manuscript (c.375) adds sugar candy (sitopalā), which closes the ancient Indian inventory of sugars.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 pp.58, 156, 166, 368 (dating Caraka ‘+1st to +2nd century’ after Basham (1) p.500, Suśruta c.+4th, Bower manuscript c.+375; Deerr (1949) pp.15–16 for the clones — Deerr not available); the texts themselves were not read. The dates of Caraka and Suśruta are layered and approximate.

entries.label: The Shuowen jiezi fixes the characters for sugarcane
entries.hint: Xu Shen’s dictionary gives the cane radical to every sugarcane name and equates zhe with zhuzhe, fixing the vocabulary the Han used for the plant in the scholarly standard of the day.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 pp.141–143 (Shuowen jiezi p.18, +121); Mazumdar (1998) p.18 (‘compiled ca. 100’).

entries.label: Galen: sakchar is less sweet than honey and not thirst-provoking
entries.hint: In his book on simple drugs Galen adds to the entry on honey that the ‘so-called sakchar’, brought from India and Arabia Felix and said to congeal on reeds, is a kind of honey: less sweet than ours but similar in power — cleansing, drying and dispersing — while not bad for the stomach, as ours is, nor thirst-provoking (the grammar of the last clause is awkward in the Greek). He repeats report (‘as they say’), not experience.
entries.note: ANCHOR (edition read): Galen, De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus 7.9 (Kühn XII.71), Greek read in the First1KGreek TEI edition (tlg0057.tlg075); also Therapeutic Method 9.4 (Kühn X.568.1), cited by Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.22 but not read. Mintz (1985) p.20 calls Galen’s mentions ‘rare and vague’. IDENTITY CONTESTED (tabasheer).

entries.label: The Nanfang caomu zhuang: Jiaozhi cane and shi mi
entries.hint: The earliest botanical account of sugarcane in the Chinese south: zhuzhe, also called ganzhe, grown in Jiaozhi with stalks several cun round and over a zhang tall, very sweet; southerners say it cures the effects of wine; and juice left in the sun for some days forms a malt-like mass that some call shi mi.
entries.note: SECONDARY (text quoted via Needham): Needham SCC 6.3 pp.67–68, 143 (NFTMC shang pp.4b–5a; authenticity discussed in SCC vol.6 pt.1 pp.447ff); Laufer (1919) p.376; Mazumdar (1998) pp.17–19 (‘ca. 305’, and the suggestion that ganzhe may be a transliteration of khaṇḍa); Needham reads kan as ‘sweet’ and Kieschnick (p.256) derives ganzhe from phāṇita — the etymology is disputed.

entries.label: Oribasius reproduces Galen; Alexander of Tralles omits sugar
entries.hint: Julian’s physician Oribasius copies Galen’s remarks on sakchar into his Medical Collections, and the later Byzantine Paul of Aegina does the same, while Alexander of Tralles, a clinician of great pharmacological experience, never mentions the substance — it remains a bookish drug, not a working one.
entries.note: ANCHOR (edition cited): Oribasius, Medical Collections 15.1, ed. Raeder, CMG 6.1.2 p.264 lines 18–22; Paul of Aegina, Epitome 7.3, ed. Heiberg II p.241 lines 3–6 (7th century, outside this folio’s window); all in Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.23, with Alexander’s omission; Dalby (2003) p.314. The ‘bookish drug’ reading is the Speculum article’s inference.

entries.label: The Armenian Geography places cane at Gundeshapur
entries.hint: A geographical text traditionally ascribed to Moses of Khorene reports sugar cane grown in Elymais near Gundeshapur and sugar ‘made artificially’ there — the earliest notice of Persian cane. Von Lippmann inferred that the Christians of Gundeshapur founded the sugar industry; Laufer calls that ‘an ingenious speculation’ not substantiated by any documents.
entries.note: SECONDARY (text not read; attribution and dating of the Armenian Geography debated): Laufer (1919) p.377 (Moses of Khorene, second half of the 5th century); Ouerfelli (2008) p.19 n.23 (Heyd, Histoire du commerce du Levant II p.681; Masuel 1937 p.2); Sato (2015) p.18. The dating should be checked against modern scholarship on the Ashkharhats’uyts.

entries.label: Sui shu: stone honey and half honey from Persia and Cao
entries.hint: The Sui shu, describing the Persia and Cao known to the Sui court, attributes to them shi mi (‘stone honey’) and ban mi (‘half honey’) — the first Chinese sign that sugar products were made west of India, though what kind of sugar is meant is not known. Dated here by what it describes, the late 6th century, not by its compilation in 636.
entries.note: SECONDARY (primary not read): Laufer (1919) p.376 nn.1–2 (Sui shu ch.83 p.7b; the earlier Wei shu ch.102 p.5b has only ‘si mi’); Sato (2015) pp.18–19 (reads ban mi as half-dried soft sugar; places Cao among the Sogdian states of Samarkand, where Laufer places Jaguda); Watson, Agricultural Innovation (1983) p.160 accepts the notice as reliable, as Sato reports. Laufer does not say the Chinese credited the Sasanians with inventing refining (as the Encyclopaedia Iranica ‘Sugar’ article paraphrases him); he calls von Lippmann’s Persian-refining theory ‘purely hypothetical’.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Honey, boiled must and maltose as the sweeteners of Rome and China; cane farms, ‘sand sugar’ and cane wine

entries.label: Roman sweeteners: honey, sapa and defrutum
entries.hint: The sweeteners a Roman farm actually produced were honey, whose bee-keeping Columella treats at length in his ninth book, and must boiled down to a syrup (defrutum and sapa), treated in the twelfth. Honey was costly and slow to make; boiled must was the cheaper sweetener. This is the market into which sakchar arrived as a medicine.
entries.note: SECONDARY (via search summaries, not read): Columella, De re rustica 9.2–16 (bees) and 12.19–21 (defrutum, sapa); Columella and Pliny assign sapa and defrutum opposite reductions (a third vs half). Date c.60. The ‘cheaper substitute’ reading comes from a modern encyclopaedic article on the syrup.

entries.label: Cane wine in India and South-East Asia
entries.loc: India; Chi-tu, the Red Earth Land, Malay peninsula
entries.hint: Cane is fermented as well as boiled: the Caraka Saṃhitā knows cane wine, the Sui shu says the people of Chi-tu on the Malay peninsula made a yellow, fragrant wine from sugar mixed with the root of a cucurbit, and a Buddhist treatise forbids cane liquor to monks as doing ‘little benefit and great harm’.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 p.58 (Caraka +1st–2nd c.; Suśruta +4th c.; Sui shu on Chi-tu); Laufer (1919) p.376 n.5 (Sui shu ch.82 p.2b); Kieschnick (2003) p.254 n.130 (Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra 13 p.158b). Nearchus’s ‘intoxicating drink’ of 325 BC belongs to the Ancient sugar folio.

entries.label: Honey and maltose, not cane, sweeten China
entries.hint: Before the Tang dynasty the Chinese kitchen was sweetened by honey and maltose, not cane: domestic bees are recorded from the end of the second century, honey sold in southern markets from the fourth, and maltose was a common Han market product. Cane sugar consumption was rare and techniques for refining it scarcely known.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Kieschnick (2003) p.254 nn.131–132 (Li Zhihuan, Zhongguo shitang shigao pp.22–59); Needham SCC 6.3 p.68; Mazumdar (1998) pp.17–22.

entries.label: Indian cane fields in Buddhist texts: irrigation and ‘red rot’
entries.hint: Buddhist texts show Indian cane farming in detail: irrigated fields, the disease known as red rot used as a simile for the danger of ordaining women, and cane grown in monastic fields; Daniels judges that ancient India was ‘without a doubt’ the first cultural area to make sugar products.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Chinese translations via Kieschnick and Daniels): Kieschnick (2003) pp.250–253 nn.108, 123 (Genben shuo yiqieyou bu pinaiye zashi 29 p.350c; Da fangdeng daji jing 11, T 397 p.67b; Haiyi pusa suowen jing 13, T 400 p.509b–c; Zhengfa nian chu jing 15 and 24); Daniels in Needham SCC 6.3 pp.191–192, 258, 367. The dates are those of the translations.

entries.label: ‘Sand sugar’ made at Guangzhou
entries.hint: The alchemist and pharmacologist Tao Hongjing (456–536) notes a cane product, shatang or ‘sand sugar’, made at Guangzhou in his day, and a Buddhist text translated in 488 confirms its prevalence there. The name suggests a dry, low-grade, granular sugar, possibly echoing Sanskrit śarkarā.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Kieschnick (2003) p.255 nn.136–137 (Tao’s gloss preserved in Li Shizhen, Bencao gangmu 33 p.12b; Shanjian lü piposha 17, T 1462 p.795b); Mazumdar (1998) p.19 (the origin of shatang from śarkarā is suggested by some scholars); Li Zhihuan, Zhongguo shitang shigao p.111 (a low-grade dry sugar).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Indian ladder from syrup to lump to crystal; the cane press; China’s sun-dried shi mi

entries.label: The Arthashastra’s ladder of cane products
entries.hint: A list in the Arthaśāstra (reported at II.15.15) names five cane products in rising purity — phāṇita (syrup), guḍa (lump jaggery), matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa and śarkarā (granulated sugar). If the list is as old as the text’s early layers, India already graded cane products by the degree of boiling before the Christian era, but the text is layered and its date contested.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Needham SCC 6.3 p.368 (guḍa already in the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra; matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa and śarkarā emerging in the Arthaśāstra, mean date 100 BC after Winter, with Caraka and Suśruta; Needham prefers the 1st century AD for these sugars); a Wisdomlib gloss citing Arthaśāstra II.15.15 (not checked); Ouerfelli (2008) p.17 (Desanges: first sugar techniques between the 4th century BC and the 1st AD); Sato (2015) p.17 (crystal sugar ‘sometime after the first century’). The sources disagree on the date.

entries.label: China dries cane juice in the sun: shi mi
entries.loc: Jiaozhi, Guangdong and the Yue south
entries.hint: Before Indian methods arrived, the Chinese south made its ‘stone honey’ by pressing cane and drying or boiling the juice in the sun, as Yang Fu described in the 1st century and Ji Han in 304. Daniels explains why nothing crystallised: until the S. barberi and S. sinense hybrids spread, cane juice rich in glucose and fructose could not be made to crystallise regularly.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Needham SCC 6.3 pp.67–68, 141 (Daniels); Mazumdar (1998) p.19 (a deep-brown raw sugar, since no source mentions separating the molasses); Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.135 (Daniels, Agro-Industries p.280). Where the techniques came from is disputed: Daniels argues the Han learned them from the non-Han peoples of the south (Kieschnick p.255 n.138), others stress India. The 647 mission to Magadha for the boiling method belongs to the Medieval sugar folio.

entries.label: The Indian cane press: mahāyantra and kolhu
entries.hint: Buddhist and Hindu texts mention a heavy cane-crushing machine, the mahāyantra, which Mazumdar identifies with the later kolhu press (the Jain texts call it kollukī); the Buddhist canon and medical treatises attest mills for crushing cane.
entries.note: SECONDARY (thin; texts not read): Needham SCC 6.3 p.290, citing Mazumdar (1984) pp.90–96 and Jain (1) for the identification, with the Jātaka mahāyantra dated about +100; Ouerfelli (2008) p.17 (Desanges (2000) p.44). The identification of the machine is Mazumdar’s suggestion.

entries.label: The three boilings: phāṇita, guḍa, śarkarā
entries.hint: A Buddhist sutra explains a monk’s progress by the refining of cane juice: boiled once it sheds its impurities (phāṇita), boiled again it grows heavy (guḍa), boiled a third time it turns white (śarkarā, rendered shimi in Chinese) — the first full description of the ladder from syrup to white sugar, as an analogy every audience was assumed to know.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Chinese translation via Kieschnick): Kieschnick (2003) pp.251–252 nn.113–116 (Zhengfa nian chu jing 3, T 721 p.17a–b, the Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra, translated in the early 6th century; Da banniepan jing 16 p.461a); Daniels in SCC 6.3 p.367. Dated by the Chinese translation; the Indian composition is earlier and uncertain.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Barygaza’s reed honey, the word’s journey, tribute cane from Funan and Jiaozhou, and the Indian physician at Gundeshapur

entries.label: ‘Honey from the reed called sacchari’ leaves Barygaza for East Africa
entries.loc: Barygaza, Bharuch and Ariaca → the Somali coast
entries.hint: Section 14 of the Periplus lists goods carried from the Indian ports of Ariaca and Barygaza to the ‘far-side’ market-towns of the African coast: wheat, rice, ghee, sesame oil, cotton cloth and girdles, and ‘honey from the reed called sacchari’. It is the only trade record of cane honey in the period; Ouerfelli reads it as cane juice or syrup, not refined sugar.
entries.note: ANCHOR (text read): Periplus Maris Erythraei 14, read verbatim in Schoff’s 1912 translation (the one occurrence of sacchari in the text); Ouerfelli (2008) p.18; Dalby (2003) p.314. The Speculum article (Bouras-Vallianatos 2021 n.21, citing Casson 1989 p.58) describes it as an export from Barygaza to the Arabian peninsula, whereas the Schoff text names the African ports — check Casson. The Periplus is dated c.40–70 (Casson), 60–70 (Shitomi, per Needham p.368) or 80–89 (McCrindle). Ouerfelli (p.18, citing Desanges 2000 pp.47–48) adds that from before the middle of the 1st century AD knowledge of India grows through commercial contacts via the Red Sea, and the testimony on cane becomes more precise, notably in Dioscorides.

entries.label: A word travels: śarkarā, sakkharā, sákchar, saccharum
entries.hint: Sanskrit śarkarā (‘grit’, granulated sugar) becomes Pali and Prakrit sakkharā and Greek sákchar, sákcharon in Dioscorides, Galen and Pliny and Latin saccharum: the word of the Indian grades of sugar reaches the Mediterranean medicine chest centuries before the product becomes common.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Dalby (2003) p.314 (the Greek is borrowed from Pali or Prakrit sakkhara); Bouras-Vallianatos, Speculum 96 (2021) n.21 (Liddell–Scott 9th ed. p.1581; Oxford Latin Dictionary s.v. sacc(h)aron); Mazumdar (1998) p.19 and Kieschnick (2003) p.256 on the Chinese terms. The word’s history does not settle what the early Greek and Latin texts mean.

entries.label: Cane syrup tribute from Jiaozhou in the Wu treasury
entries.hint: The Sanguozhi tells how Sun Liang of Wu sent a eunuch to the palace warehouse for cane syrup (tang) that had come as tribute from Jiaozhou, and discovered that the keeper had mixed rat droppings into it — a southern product stored as a tributary luxury at the Wu court in the middle of the 3rd century.
entries.note: SECONDARY (primary not read): Sanguo zhi (Chen Shou, c.233–297), as translated by Mazumdar (1998) p.19 n.29, who dates the anecdote only to ‘a period a bit past the turn of the third century’; Sun Liang reigned 252–258.

entries.label: An Indian physician is brought to Gundeshapur
entries.hint: Arabic sources say Shapur I founded Gundeshapur and brought a physician from India to teach medicine there; the people of Susa learned the art well and became the most reputed physicians. In Mintz’s account Gondeshapur is later one of the principal centres through which sugar entered the medical tradition, but no source ties this physician, or Shapur’s time, to sugar.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Arabic traditions via Ouerfelli): Ouerfelli (2008) p.19 n.25 (al-Tabari, Ta’rikh II p.845; al-Tha’alibi, Ghurar p.531); Mintz (1985) p.21 on Gondeshapur as a centre of the transmission of sugar lore in the Islamic period. Context only: no sugar is attested.

entries.label: Funan sends giant cane to the Jin court
entries.hint: In the sixth year of Taikang the kingdom of Funan presented to the Western Jin court sugarcane with three nodes to the zhang — a Mekong-delta cane notable for its size, probably a thick S. officinarum type, and a gift Chinese writers repeat for the next century.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Ji Han, Nanfang caomu zhuang shang p.4b, as given in Needham SCC 6.3 pp.63, 143 (+285; the OCR of one passage reads +283); Laufer (1919) p.376 (285); Mazumdar (1998) p.19 and Sato (2015) p.17 give 286; Needham identifies the cane as S. officinarum but notes the circumference measure could fit S. sinense.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Han absorb Nanyue; the monsoon route to India

entries.label: Han absorbs Nanyue — and learns of southern cane
entries.hint: After the Han conquered the southern kingdom of Nanyue in 111 BC, Chinese poets and officials reached the lands of the hundred Yue and began to write about sugarcane; Daniels proposes that references to cane begin to appear in Chinese literature because of these conquests of the southern Yue.
entries.note: SECONDARY (the conquest is standard background): Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.133 (Daniels, Agro-Industries pp.182–183; Li Zhihuan pp.66–69); Needham SCC 6.3 p.141 (officials reached the Yue south ‘around −200’). Cane did not come to China from India: it was a southern Yue crop before it was a Han text.

entries.label: The monsoon route to India
entries.loc: Red Sea ports of Roman Egypt to the Indian west coast
entries.hint: Greek and Roman captains learn to ride the south-west monsoon straight across the Indian Ocean — the ‘Hippalus’ wind — making the voyage between Egypt and the Indian ports seasonal and routine. It is the context for how any Indian product reached Roman writers, sakchar among them; no source ties it to sugar directly.
entries.note: CONTEXT (via search summaries; Periplus 57 not read here): the Periplus credits Hippalus with the open-sea route, Pliny the wind; Hippalus is placed in the 1st century BC (Tchernia reconciles the two), and Tripati (2011) argues that Indian mariners rode the monsoon earlier. The date is approximate.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The southern Yue and the deportees of Khuzestan

entries.label: The southern Yue and their cane
entries.loc: Lingnan and Jiaozhi, Guangdong to Tonkin
entries.hint: Sugarcane was part of the diet of the Yue peoples of the south before Han writers noticed it, and Han immigrants adopted the practice; cane was not originally a Han crop. The Han policy of sinicising the Yue met repeated rebellions and was softened in 136 AD by appointing local leaders — the people who grew the cane appear in the record chiefly as a frontier to be governed.
entries.note: SECONDARY (back-projection flagged): Needham SCC 6.3 pp.58, 62, 66 (the Yue diet; Han policy; the 136 date comes from an OCR passage and should be checked); Kieschnick (2003) p.255 n.133; the modern ritual use of cane in south China (Anderson & Anderson, cited by Needham p.62) is a speculative back-projection and is not claimed for this period. Daniels argues that the Han Chinese first learned the techniques for making amorphous sugar from the non-Han peoples of the south (Kieschnick p.255 n.138; Daniels, Agro-Industries p.88).

entries.label: Deportees and Roman prisoners remake Khuzestan
entries.hint: Arabic tradition says Shapur I resettled captive populations at Susa and Tustar, where weaving of brocades, silks and carpets began, and set Valerian’s Roman prisoners to build the great weir at Shushtar — forced labour at the origin of the irrigated province that later grew Persia’s cane.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Arabic traditions via Ouerfelli): Ouerfelli (2008) pp.19–20 nn.24–27 (al-Mas’udi, Muruj I p.299; al-Tha’alibi, Ghurar pp.527–528; Ibn Hawqal; al-Idrisi). The link from these works to cane is Ouerfelli’s conjecture; for Shapur and Valerian see sassanid-224-484 and roman-sasanian-world-224-632.
